analytic.title: Hierarchical Real-Time Scheduling Framework for Imprecise Computations *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Hierarchical scheduling frameworks provide ways for composing large and complex real-time systems from independent sub-systems. In this paper, we consider the imprecise reward-based periodic task model in a compositional scheduling framework. Thus, we introduce the imprecise periodic resource model to characterize the imprecise resource allocations, and the interface model to abstract the imprecise real-time requirements of the component. The schedulability analysis of mandatory parts is analyzed to meet the minimum requirement of tasks. In addition, we provide a scheduling algorithm for guaranteeing a certain amount of reward, which makes it feasible to compose multiple imprecise components efficiently.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: To build large complex real-time systems, componentbased design has been widely accepted as methodology for composing the system through systematic abstraction and composition. Component-based design provides a means for decomposing a system into components, allowing the reduction of a single complex design problem to multiple simpler design problems, and composing components into a system through component interfaces that abstract and hide their internal complexity. Component-based design also facilitates the reuse of components that may have been developed in different environments.

In a compositional real-time scheduling framework, the main problem is to define a scheduling interface model in order to specify the collective real-time requirements of a component. Many frameworks [1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,11] have been proposed for different real-time models. In [2], a hierarchical real-time virtual resource model that permits resource partitioning to be extended to multiple levels is introduced. Through this model, partitions on each level are scheduled as if they had access to a dedicated resource and there is minimal interference between neighboring partition levels. In [3,5,8], a periodic resource model is proposed to handle the periodic task model [12] in a compositional hierarchical scheduling framework. Their periodic resource model describes a behavior of a periodic resource and calculates its minimum resource allocations. Shin and Lee [6] extended this framework to support the bounded-delay task model [13] and developed an exact schedulability condition. In [4], a framework for compositional and hierarchical realtime scheduling is proposed to permit resource partitioning to be extended to multiple levels and handle a wider range of scheduling algorithms and task models. A hierarchical scheduling framework is also proposed for virtual clustering of multiprocessors [7]. The scheduling framework presented in [9] considers various kinds of real-time guarantees. This work focuses principally on converting one kind of guarantee into another kind of guarantee such that whenever the former is satisfied, the later is also satisfied.

In most real-time systems, each task must complete and produce correct results by specified deadlines. However, for many recent applications, such as audio/video processing, system control and navigation systems, approximate results are acceptable within some penalties. For these purposes, imprecise computation [14,15] and IRIS (Increased Reward with Increased Service) [16] task models were proposed to enhance resource utilization and reduce penalties associated with incomplete task accomplishment. In these models every real-time task is composed of a mandatory part and an optional part. The former must be completed by the task's deadline to provide minimal acceptable output. The optional part, on the other hand, can be executed after the mandatory part before the deadline if the system resources allow. Rewards are also associated with the completed portion of the optional part with the objective of maximizing the total reward.

In this paper, we propose a new hierarchical real-time framework for composing imprecise computation tasks, and a scheduling algorithm in the model. The main contributions of our work are: (i) to provide a new compositional framework for imprecise computations, (ii) to analyze the schedulability of mandatory requirements of a component, and (iii) to provide a scheduling algorithm for guaranteeing a certain amount of reward.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the proposed compositional real-time scheduling framework. The imprecise resource model is detailed in Section 3. The schedulability of mandatory parts is analyzed in Section 4. Section 5 presents a scheduling algorithm to guarantee a reward. We evaluate the proposed algorithm throughout numerical analysis and simulations in Section 6. Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper.

div.head: Compositional Framework for Imprecise Computation
div.p: The basic unit of scheduling in a compositional or hierarchical scheduling framework is called a scheduling component and is defined as a triple of C(W, R, A), where W is the set of workloads in the component, R is the resource model specifying the resource allocations available to the component, and A is the scheduling algorithm inside the component [6]. Scheduling components are organized in a tree-like structure, in which a parent component allocates resource to its child component as shown in Figure 1. In this section, we propose a new compositional scheduling framework for imprecise computation model. So, we define resource model and interface model for the compositional framework.

div.head: Task and Resource Models
div.p: A component workload W consists of n periodic imprecise computation tasks. Each task τ i is characterized by (p i , m i , o i , f i ). That is, task τ i releases a job every p i time units. The relative deadline of the job is equal to its period. The computation time of a job is divided into two parts: a mandatory part (m i ) and an optional part (o i ). The mandatory part must meet its deadline to provide minimal acceptable service, while the optional part can be executed for the additional improvement of quality if the system resource is available. Such improvement is defined by the reward function f i . When a job of τ i executes t time units for its optional part, the reward R i (t) is defined as follows.
div.formula: R i (t) = f i (t) if 0 ≤ t ≤ o i f i (o i ) if t > o i
div.p: We note that f i (t) is a nondecreasing function; thus, the reward of a task τ i cannot decrease by allowing the task to run longer. Likewise, the reward accrued by a task τ i ceases to increase when its optional part's execution time t reaches its worst-case value o i . As a resource model, we propose a new periodic resource model to handle the requirements of the imprecise computation model. The imprecise resource model detailed in Section 3, is defined as Γ(Π, Θ, Ω), where Π is a resource period (Π > 0), Θ is the periodic resource allocation time for the mandatory part (0 < Θ ≤ Π), and Ω the periodic resource allocation for the optional part (0 ≤ Ω, Θ+Ω ≤ Π).

div.head: Interface Model
div.p: The real-time requirement of a component C(W, R, A) is specified by the real-time interface I without any internal information about the component [8]. With no consideration of their internal information such as their workloads and algorithms, the scheduler of an upper layer component is able to schedule its child components using their interfaces.

The interface model for the proposed compositional framework is defined as I(P, M, O, F ), where P is the period, M the mandatory execution time requirement, O the optional execution time requirement, and F the reward function of optional execution time. Since a component is considered as one imprecise task by the upper layer scheduler, the interface model accords with the imprecise task model specification.

div.head: Framework Overview
div.p: An overview of the proposed framework is illustrated by the example of Figure 1. Component C 1 has two imprecise computation tasks under Mandatory-First Earliest Deadline First (MF-EDF) scheduling algorithm [14,15]. Interface I 1 is derived from the characteristics of C 1 . Similarly, interface I 2 is derived from the component C 2 which have two imprecise computation tasks under Mandatory-First Rate Monotonic (MF-RM) algorithm [14,15]. These two interfaces are converted as corresponding tasks (τ 5 and τ 6 ) for the upper layer component C 0 . Now, component C 0 focuses on scheduling these two tasks without consideration of the two lower layer components. Indeed, component C 0 does not need to collect internal scheduling information such as the number of tasks and the scheduling policy about its child components. As a result of scheduling in C 0 , imprecise resource supply R 1 and R 2 are allocated to its child components C 1 and C 2 , respectively.

div.head: Application Domains
div.p: The proposed hierarchical scheduling framework can be applied to many applications based on imprecise computation model. Such applications include audio/video processing, multimedia data streaming [11], real-time image tracking, and so on. The overload system management can also use the framework, since the imprecise computation model was proposed not only to provide hard real-time guarantees to a task but also to enhance the resource utilization when the system is overloaded.

Furthermore, the proposed compositional framework improves the performance of those applications by leveraging recent technologies related to compositional platforms. For example, multicore real-time scheduling algorithms may use the proposed model for partitioning and scheduling a group of imprecise computation tasks. In virtualized platforms, a group of imprecise computation applications may run on a single virtual machine. Hypervisor schedulers, such as Xen Hypervisor [17], can use the proposed framework in allocating the CPU resource to multiple virtual machines.

div.head: Problem Description
div.p: Many issues should be solved in the proposed framework. In this paper, we consider the following problems and propose some solutions.
• Modeling of imprecise resource: The compositional framework should provide a resource model to abstract the resource supply to an imprecise computation-based component (see in Section 3).

• Schedulability analysis: In order to guarantee the minimum requirement of a component, schedulability analysis is required. Utilization bound analysis also provides useful information for the schedulability analysis (see in Section 4).

div.head: Imprecise Resource Model
div.p: A resource model specifies the amount of resource to be allocated to each component. In order to provide a seamless composition of imprecise computation tasks, we propose a new resource model in the framework. The imprecise resource model is defined as Γ(Π, Θ, Ω), where Π is a resource period (Π > 0), Θ is the mandatory resource allocation time per period (0 < Θ ≤ Π), and Ω the optional resource allocation time per period (0 ≤ Ω, Θ + Ω ≤ Π). The imprecise resource model Γ(Π, Θ, Ω) periodically supplies at least Θ time units and at most Θ+Ω time units if the resource is available. Figure 2 shows an example of the imprecise resource model. Thus, the periodic resource model in [8] is a special case of Ω = 0 in our model. The resource supply of Γ(Π, Θ, Ω) is characterized by the following.
div.formula: Θ ≤ supply Γ (kΠ, (k+1)Π) ≤ Θ+Ω, where k = 0, 1, 2, . . .(1)
div.p: Example 3.1 In Figure 1, the imprecise resource supply R 1 = Γ(10, 3, 2) provided by the component C 0 to its child C 1 guarantees a mandatory part of 3 computational time units every period of 10 time units. At the same time, if the resources are available, C 0 may provide more resource up to 2 time units to C 1 .

div.head: Schedulability Test
div.p: An imprecise computation task is said to be schedulable if every mandatory part is guaranteed to complete before the deadline. For the schedulability analysis, we use the minimum resource supply of a component resource model.

Scheduling algorithms of imprecise computation tasks are classified into two approaches: mandatory first and coupling ones. Mandatory First (MF) policy [14,15] executes mandatory parts of all tasks and then maximizes the system reward by scheduling optional parts. On the contrary, coupling approach [18] statically determines the optimal execution time of each task's optional part [18] and schedules tasks using any scheduling algorithm, such as EDF or RM (Rate Monotonic).

In order to analyze the schedulability of mandatory parts in compositional framework, we use the Mandatory First (MF) approach. Since mandatory parts have higher priorities than any optional parts in MF policy, the schedulability analysis only considers m i of each task τ i . An imprecise resource model Γ(Π, Θ, Ω) guarantees only the mandatory resource supply of Θ time units every Π time units. Therefore, the problem of schedulability analysis is reduced to the same one as in [8]. We define the resource demand [5] of a workload set as the amount of resource allocation that the workload requests. The resource demand bound function dbf W (A, t) of a time interval t calculates the maximum resource demand for the mandatory subset of the workload under the scheduling policy A. The following proposition provides the schedulability of a component for a given imprecise resource supply under MF-EDF (Mandatory First Earliest Deadline First) policy. For the proof, we can apply m i instead of e i in Theorem 4.1 in [8].

div.head: Proposition 1 (Scheduability of MF-EDF) A component C(W, R, A
div.p: ) is schedulable for a given resource R = Γ(Π, Θ, Ω), where W = {τ i (p i , m i , o i , f i )} and A = MF-EDF, if and only if,
div.formula: dbf W (A, t) = τi∈W t/p i • m i ≤ sbf Γ (t),
div.p: for all t such that 0 < t ≤ LCM W , where LCM W is the least common multiple of p i for all τ i ∈ W .
Similarly, Proposition 2 gives the schedulability analysis of a component under MF-FP (Mandatory First Fixed Priority) scheduling algorithms, as a result of Theorem 4.2 in [8].

div.p: ) is schedulable for a given resource R = Γ(Π, Θ, Ω), where W = {τ i (p i , m i , o i , f i )} and A = MF-FP, if and only if, for all τ i ∈ W , there exists t ∈ [0, p i ] such that
div.formula: dbf W (A, t) = m i + τ k ∈HPW (i) t/p k • m k ≤ sbf Γ (t),
div.p: where HP W (i) is the set of higher-priority tasks than τ i in W . 4. Thus, all mandatory parts of the component are guaranteed to meet their deadlines.

The imprecise resource model specifies not only minimum resource supply, but also additional resource allocation. Thus, a component of which schedulability is not guaranteed with the minimum resource supply, can be scheduled at the run-time. For this reason, we define weakly schedulability of a component in the imprecise resource model. Definition 4.1 For a resource supply R = Γ(Π, Θ, Ω), a component C(W, R, A) is said to be weakly schedulable if there exists Ω ≤ Ω such that the component is schedulable under R = Γ(Π, Θ + Ω , Ω -Ω ).

A weakly schedulable component can meet all mandatory parts if additional resource supply of Ω time units is given consistently per resource period. The weakly schedulability test is determined by usbf(t).

div.head: Proposition 3 (Weakly Scheduability) A component C(W, R, A) is weakly schedulable for a given resource
div.formula: R = Γ(Π, Θ, Ω), where W = {τ i (p i , m i , o i , f i )}, if and only if, dbf W (A, t) ≤ usbf Γ (t),
div.p: for all t such that 0 < t ≤ LCM W , where LCM W is the least common multiple of p i for all τ i ∈ W .

Example 4.2 Let us consider a component C 2 with two tasks, τ 1 (9, 2, 3) and τ 2 (15,3,4) for a given imprecise resource Γ(5, 2, 1). The upper bound of minimum resource supply of Γ, usbf(t), is shown in Figure 4. The mandatory resource demand bound function, dbf(t), of C 2 under MF-EDF is always smaller than or equal to usbf(t), as shown in Figure 4. C 2 is not guaranteed to be schedulable with the minimum supply, because there exist some points where dbf(t) > sbf(t). However, C 2 can be schedulable by additional resource supply of the resource model. So, it is weakly schedulable by the resource model.

The weakly schedulability test is used in two-folds. First, the upper layer component can provide Ω more to a weakly schedulable component to make it schedulable. Second, weakly hard real-time systems [19,20,21] can use this analysis in compositional framework. Many recent real-time applications are hard but sometimes allow occasional misses of deadlines, which are said to be weakly hard. A weakly schedulable component completes their mandatory parts with occasional deadline misses. If a component consists of weakly hard real-time tasks, then the weakly schedulability may be enough to satisfy the weakly hard constraints.

div.head: Utilization Bound
div.p: Given an imprecise resource model Γ(Π, Θ, Ω), the utilization bound U B Γ (A) of a scheduling algorithm A is defined as a number such that the component C(W, Γ, A) is schedulable if the workload mandatory utilization is no greater than the utilization bound, that is,
div.formula: τi∈W m i p i ≤ U B Γ (A).
div.p: Similarly, the weakly utilization bound W UB Γ (A) of a scheduling algorithm A is defined as a number such that the component C(W, Γ, A) is weakly schedulable if the workload mandatory utilization is no greater than the utilization bound, that is,
div.formula: τi∈W m i p i ≤ W UB Γ (A).
div.p: Considering a component C(W, Γ(Π, Θ, Ω), MF-EDF), since the imprecise resource model guarantees only the mandatory resource supply, the utilization bound under MF-EDF for the mandatory part is given by
div.formula: U B W (EDF ) = Θ Π 1 - 2(Π -Θ) p *(4)
div.p: where p * is the smallest period in the workload W [5].
Similarly, the weakly utilization bound of MF-EDF is defined by

div.head: Scheduling with Reward Guarantee
div.p: Generally, a component scheduler allocates more resource to a lower-layer component which provides more reward while guaranteeing all mandatory parts. In this section, we derive the minimum reward of a component for a given imprecise resource supply, and propose a scheduling algorithm to guarantee such minimum reward. Definition 5.1 For a given imprecise resource supply R = Γ(Π, Θ, Ω), a minimum reward of a component C(W, R, A) is defined as a guaranteed reward that a component provides under the imprecise resource supply Γ(Π, Θ, Ω).

In order to guarantee both mandatory part execution and a certain amount of reward, we statically determine an optional execution time of each task and give it the same priority as the mandatory part. The following optimization problem, denoted as MAX-CREW, is used to decide such optional execution time for the purpose of maximizing the guaranteed reward per unit time:
div.formula: M aximize τi∈W f i (õ i ) p i Subject to τi∈W (m i + õi ) p i ≤ U B Γ (A) 0 ≤ õi ≤ o i , i = 1, . . . , |W |(6)
div.p: where õi represents the amount of computational time allocated to task τ i , 0 ≤ õi ≤ o i .
As the utilization bound of EDF is given by Equation ( 4), the minimum reward under EDF is calculated by solving the following optimization problem, denoted as MAX-CREW EDF :
div.formula: M aximize τi∈W f i (õ i ) p i Subject to τi∈W õi p i ≤ Θ Π 1 - 2(Π -Θ) p * - τi∈W m i p i 0 ≤ õi ≤ o i , i = 1, . . . , |W |(7)
div.p: MAX-CREW EDF can be solved using the method of Lagrangian multipliers [22] under the assumption that the reward functions are differentiable, concave and nondecreasing on their domains. First, we derive an intermediate solution to the problem by ignoring the inactive constraints and considering only active constraints, i.e. considering the equality in the constraints. And then, the solution is refined by considering all the conditions including inequality conditions. This technique can provide the result in O(n 2 log n), where n = |W |. Once the minimum reward is computed and every õi is determined, each task τ i is then scheduled as a new imprecise computation task with mandatory execution time of m i + õi , and optional execution time of o i -õi . After then, the mandatory first scheduling algorithm (ex. MF-EDF) not only meets all the mandatory execution but also guarantees f i (õ i ) reward every Π time units.

div.head: Performance Evaluation
div.p: We evaluated the proposed algorithm on a component with the workload comprised of five tasks as shown in Table 1. We consider exponential, logarithmic and linear reward functions as reward functions, since they are concave, differentiable, and nondecreasing. The resource supply period is fixed as 5 time units throughout the evaluation. The scheduling algorithm is based on MF-EDF in the evaluation.

div.head: Numerical Analysis of Minimum Reward
div.p: We fixed the resource supply period (Π) as 5 time units and varied the mandatory resource supply (Ω) from 1.75 to 4.5 time units. The minimum guaranteed reward is obtained by solving Equation (7). Figure 5 shows the minimum reward per unit time accrued by the component for the three function sets. Figure 5 also includes the minimum reward of each task τ i in each case. As more resource is supplied, the component guarantees more reward.

After some points, (e.g. 3.75 time units in Figure 5), the reward does not change because the resource supply is enough to schedule all optional parts of the component. For example, Figure 6 shows the guaranteed optional execution time of each task, õi , in the case of logarithmic reward functions. As shown in Figure 6, all the optional parts are executed after 3.75 time units of mandatory resource supply.

When an upper-layer component shares its resource to multiple lower-layer components, a resource allocation policy is required to share the limited resource efficiently. One metric is the guaranteed reward per resource supply, so that the component allocates more resource to a lowerlayer component with higher such metric value. div.head: Simulation Results
div.p: We compared the proposed scheduling algorithm with MF-EDF throughout simulations. We simulated the task set of Table 1 on its hyperperiod (=25200) by varying the resource supply from 1.75 to 4.50 time units. We consider the total reward accrued by the system for each resource supply. The proposed algorithm statically computes the minimum reward and determines the optional parts which will be scheduled together with the mandatory parts.

Figure 8 shows average reward per resource supply for each resource supply. As shown in Figure 8, the proposed algorithm provides more reward than MF-EDF since it schedules pre-determined optional parts without missing mandatory part deadlines.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we proposed a new hierarchical scheduling framework for imprecise computation tasks. The framework includes imprecise resource model and interface model. Schedulability analysis is provided for guaranteeing mandatory parts of components. In addition, we derived optional execution times to maximize the total reward for a given resource supply, and suggested a scheduling algorithm with guarantee of such reward. The proposed framework and algorithm can be used for efficient composition of multiple imprecise computations on many recent hierarchical platforms, such as multicores and virtualization technology. We will investigate many interesting problems on the proposed framework, such as deriving component interface, analysis of weakly hard constraints, and optimal scheduling of optional parts.
